entries.meaning: Rama describes true friendship: share a friend's pain, restrain wrongdoing, disclose virtues, conceal faults, give without suspicion, and show hundredfold affection in adversity; abandon the flattering but inwardly crooked friend. Sugriva tests Rama's power, then turns toward renunciation, but Rama reminds him that his promise to kill Bali cannot be false. Sugriva challenges Bali; Tara warns that Rama and Lakshmana stand behind him, but Bali proudly goes out, saying that even death at impartial Rama's hand would give him a true Lord.

Bali proudly attacks Sugriva, whom he considers no more than straw. Sugriva flees after a thunderbolt-like blow and protests to Rama. Rama explains that the brothers looked identical, strengthens Sugriva's body, and marks him with a flower garland. In the renewed combat Rama watches from behind a tree; when Sugriva's strength and stratagems fail, he draws an arrow and strikes Bali through the heart.

Mortally wounded, Bali recognizes Rama yet asks why an incarnation of righteousness killed him like a hunter while favouring Sugriva. Rama answers that a younger brother's wife, sister, son's wife, and unmarried girl are to be regarded as daughters; Bali lustfully seized one, ignored Tara's warning, and attacked a man sheltered by Rama. Bali concedes that cleverness cannot prevail before his Lord and asks for Rama as his final refuge.

Moved by Bali's tender words, Rama touches his head and offers to make his body sound and preserve his life. Bali declines: sages labour through many births yet may not utter Rama's name at death, while the very Lord whose name grants the imperishable state at Kashi now stands before his eyes. Such an opportunity, he asks, could never come again.

Rama sends Bali to his own divine abode. Tara rushes out in grief, but Rama teaches her that the lowly body is made of earth, water, fire, ether, and air: the visible body lies before her, while the soul is eternal. Enlightened, she asks for supreme devotion. Sugriva performs Bali's rites, and Lakshmana installs Sugriva as king and Angada as crown prince.

Shiva tells Uma that no worldly relation is as beneficent as Rama, since others commonly love for self-interest. Rama's natural compassion raised the terrified, wounded Sugriva to kingship. Rama instructs him in statecraft, explains that his fourteen-year vow bars him from cities, and retires to Mount Pravarshana for the rainy season while Sugriva rules with Angada and remembers Rama's task.
